questions.stem: The electron configuration of an atom of chlorine, atomic number 17, is
questions.explanation: Filling shells from the inside out, the first shell takes 2 electrons and the second takes 8, leaving 17 - 10 = 7 for the third shell. Seven outer electrons place chlorine in group VII, which is why it needs just one more electron to complete its octet.

distractorRationale.b: Shells must be filled to capacity in order, so the second shell cannot stop at 7 while the third has 8
distractorRationale.c: This is potassium with 19 electrons
distractorRationale.d: The first shell holds a maximum of 2 electrons, not 8

questions.stem: Potassium has atomic number 19. Its correct electron configuration is 2, 8, 8, 1 rather than 2, 8, 9 because

options.text: the third shell can never hold more than 8 electrons
the 4s subshell is lower in energy than the 3d subshell, so it fills first
potassium is a metal and metals always have one outer electron
the nineteenth electron is repelled out of the atom

questions.explanation: By the Aufbau principle electrons occupy the lowest available energy subshell. Although 3d belongs to the third shell, its energy is slightly above that of 4s, so the nineteenth electron enters 4s and the configuration becomes 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1.

distractorRationale.a: The third shell holds up to 18 electrons; it simply pauses at 8 until 4s is filled
distractorRationale.c: Metals have varying numbers of outer electrons, for example magnesium has two
distractorRationale.d: All 19 electrons remain bound in a neutral potassium atom

questions.stem: The rule stating that electrons occupy the orbitals of a subshell singly before pairing up is
questions.explanation: Hund's rule says electrons spread out among degenerate orbitals with parallel spins first, because keeping them in separate orbitals minimises the repulsion between them. Only when every orbital of the subshell holds one electron does pairing begin.

distractorRationale.a: The Aufbau principle governs the order in which subshells are filled, not the arrangement within one subshell
distractorRationale.c: The Pauli exclusion principle limits an orbital to two electrons of opposite spin
distractorRationale.d: The octet rule concerns the eight outer electrons atoms aim for during bonding

questions.stem: An element X has the electron configuration 2, 8, 2. To which period and group of the periodic table does X belong?
questions.explanation: Three shells are occupied, so the element lies in period 3. There are two electrons in the outermost shell, so it lies in group II. The element is magnesium, atomic number 12, which readily loses those two electrons to form Mg2+.

distractorRationale.a: The period was read as the number of full inner shells rather than the total number of occupied shells
distractorRationale.c: The group was read as the number of shells rather than the number of outer electrons
distractorRationale.d: The atomic number was mistaken for the period number

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct electron configuration of the Fe2+ ion, given that iron has atomic number 26?
questions.explanation: Neutral iron is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d6 4s2. Although 4s fills before 3d, the 4s electrons are further from the nucleus and are removed first when an ion forms. Losing both 4s electrons gives Fe2+ as 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d6.

distractorRationale.b: The two electrons were removed from 3d instead of 4s
distractorRationale.c: This is the neutral iron atom with 26 electrons, not the 2+ ion with 24
distractorRationale.d: Electrons cannot enter 4p while 3d is still empty, since 3d is lower in energy

questions.stem: Noble gases are chemically unreactive mainly because they have

options.text: equal numbers of protons and neutrons
no electrons in their outer shell

questions.explanation: A filled outer shell, two electrons for helium and eight for the others, is an especially stable low-energy arrangement. Because there is nothing to gain by transferring or sharing electrons, noble gas atoms have almost no tendency to form bonds.

distractorRationale.a: Noble gases actually have small radii compared with the group I metals of the same period
distractorRationale.c: Equal proton and neutron numbers have no bearing on chemical reactivity
distractorRationale.d: Noble gases have full outer shells, not empty ones
